item.title: I tested 5 minimalist notes apps, and this one actually stuck
item.itunes:title: I tested 5 minimalist notes apps, and this one actually stuck
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have tried plenty of notes apps, but most of them eventually started feeling like too much. I don't always need folders, databases, templates, or a long list of settings just to save a thought. Sometimes, I just want to open an app and write.

So, I decided to try five minimalist notes apps and use them for my everyday notes. I wanted to see which one felt simple enough to use regularly without becoming frustrating. I used each app for quick thoughts, lists, and things I wanted to remember. By the end, one app stood out enough that I decided to keep it.

Notally

Just notes, nothing more

Notally was one of the first apps I tried because it feels like it knows exactly what a notes app should be. There is no learning curve or complicated setup. I opened it, created a note, and started typing. The interface is clean without feeling too bare, and everything is where I expected it to be. I also liked how quickly I could move between individual notes and my overall list.

It felt more like a digital notepad than a full productivity system, which was exactly what I wanted from a minimalist app. The experience stayed focused on writing rather than making me manage the app itself. After a few days, though, I started noticing where its simplicity could become limiting. It was great for quick thoughts and temporary notes, but I wasn't sure it would become my everyday notes app.

Simplenote

The one that kept things simple

Simplenote felt like a good fit when I wanted something simple that still worked across my devices. I liked that my notes synced quickly, so I could start something on my laptop and pick it up later on my phone without thinking about it. The tag system was also useful. Instead of creating folders for everything, I could add a few tags and use them to find related notes later. Global search made this even easier when I couldn't remember which tag I had used.

I also liked the Markdown support. It gave me a simple way to format notes without adding a lot of buttons or menus to the editor. The version history was another feature I found useful because I could look back at older versions of a note if I changed something by mistake. Simplenote stayed very lightweight while still giving me these useful features, which made it one of the more practical apps I tested.

I chose the perfect note-taking app for my work style, and here's how you can too

Don't make the wrong choice

2
By  Sumukh Rao

Easy Notes

More than just a simple notepad

Easy Notes caught my attention with a few features that made it different from the other apps I tested. I could lock individual notes with a password, which was useful when I wanted to keep certain information private. The app also lets me add photos to notes, so I could keep an image with the related text instead of saving them separately. I found the voice input option useful too when typing wasn't convenient. I could simply speak and get the note down quickly.

Another small feature I liked was the ability to set reminders for notes. This worked well for things I needed to remember later but didn't want to move into a separate reminder app. Easy Notes also gives me different ways to sort and view my notes, which helped when I had more of them. These aren't advanced features, but they made the app feel more useful than a basic text notepad.

Notesnook

The minimalist app with privacy

Notesnook felt a little more feature-rich than the other minimalist apps I tested. What stood out to me most was its focus on privacy. It uses end-to-end encryption, so my notes stay protected when they sync across devices. I also liked the editor. I could add headings, lists, quotes, and basic formatting without the app feeling too complicated.

It also lets me organize notes into notebooks, which was useful when I had several notes around the same topic. I could also add reminders to notes, so I didn't always need a separate reminder app. Another nice touch was its support for themes and customization, letting me change the way the app looked. It wasn't as bare as Notally or Simplenote, but it still felt easy enough for everyday note-taking.

HedgeDoc

When notes become a shared workspace

HedgeDoc was the odd one out in my test because it felt more like a shared writing space than a regular notes app. I liked that I could create a document and work on it directly from the browser without installing anything. The live preview was especially useful when writing in Markdown. I could see how the finished document would look while I was still editing it.

Collaboration was another feature I noticed quickly. I could share a document with someone else and work on it together, which made HedgeDoc useful for meeting notes, plans, or quick drafts. It also supports comments and lets me see who is editing the document. I liked the simplicity, but HedgeDoc made the most sense when I needed to write with other people rather than just keep personal notes.

5 self-hosted Evernote alternatives for next-level note-taking experience

Ditch the cloud and own your data with these next-level note apps

5
By  Yash Patel

The one that earned a permanent spot in my workflow

After testing all five apps, Simplenote was the one I kept using. It wasn't the app with the most features, but I didn't miss them. The other apps had useful features, but Simplenote felt like the best fit for how I actually take notes. What made the difference was how easy it was to use every day. I didn't have to change my habits or spend time setting things up. I could just write and find my notes when I needed them.

Simplenote

If you want a basic note-taking app that works across every platform, Simplenote is for you. It's free to download and use across platforms.

item.title: Acer’s tiny Project DualPlay Mini handheld is built for gaming and getting things done
item.itunes:title: Acer’s tiny Project DualPlay Mini handheld is built for gaming and getting things done
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Acer has shown off Project DualPlay Mini, its flip-and-swivel concept handheld that docks with a small backlit keyboard.
  • The company also revealed more about the Predator Atlas 7, its Intel Arc G3 Extreme (B390)-powered handheld with a 7-inch FHD 120Hz display and 24GB LPDDR5x. The Atlas 7 is set to release in November, but pricing is still unknown.
  • New laptops and PCs have been revealed: Vero 16 MIL-STD chassis, Switch Blade/Air with Core 7 350, SFF RTX Spark and Veriton RI110 with up to 96GB.

At IFA 2026, Acer once again showed off Project DualPlay Mini, a concept device the company has "revealed" several times over the years in various forms, including back at CES 2025 and even as far back as IFA 2024.

Acer says that the DualPlay Mini functions both as a gaming handheld and a mobile productivity station. Basically, you can use the DualPlay Mini as a more traditional Windows 11 handheld, but there's also a backlit physical keyboard you can dock it in for a more traditional laptop experience. Acer says that Project DualPlay features a "distinctive flip-and-swivel" design that easily converts between handheld and mini-laptop modes.

Credit: Acer

The concept is actually pretty compelling, and the type of device would really appeal to me personally, since I like to get work done when traveling, but also kick back and game for a bit. Acer says the Project DualPlay Mini is still just a concept device and doesn't have a release date.

While a lot of concept devices don't actually ever get released, I can see the DualPlay Mini dropping at some point, if only because Acer has shown it off so many times now, including a larger working prototype at CES 2025.

Acer revealed the smaller Predator Atlas 7 with a 7-inch screen

The company showed off several laptop hardware refreshes, too

Credit: Acer

At IFA, Acer also highlighted its Predator Atlas 7, one of the first handhelds powered by Intel's Arc G3 Extreme Chip with Intel Arc B390 graphics, featuring a 7-inch FHD 120Hz screen with 500-nit peak brightness and VRR support, TMR joysticks, 24GB LPDDR5x RAM, AeroBlade fans, and more. Acer will also offer a lower-end version of the Atlas 7 that features an Intel Arc G3 processor and an Intel Arc B370 GPU. The handheld appears nearly identical to the previously revealed Atlas 8, but with a smaller

Acer confirmed that the Predator Atlas 7 will be released in North America in November 2026, but unsurprisingly, given the ongoing RAMpocalypse, the company didn't confirm pricing. However, since it's already September, we'll know how much the Atlas 7 will cost soon enough. I bet that the Predator Atlas 7 will cost in the $1,800 range, similar to the Arc G3 Extreme-powered MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. The company also revealed that the larger Predator Atlas 8 will launch in September.

As is always the case, Acer showed off several new laptops at IFA 2026, including the Acer Vero 16, a heavy-duty laptop with a MIL-STD-810 certified chassis and up to an Intel Core Ultra X9 388H processor, and its lightweight Switch Blade 14 and Switch Air 16, which feature Intel's Core 7 350 Processor.

Acer also revealed its SFF RTX Spark, a compact, AI-focused desktop that's powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark chip, and its Veriton R10 AI Mini Workstation, which features an Intel Core Ultra X 358H processor, an Intel Arc B390 GPU, and up to 96GB of LPDDR5X RAM.

Asus' New ProArt P16 and P14 pack Nvidia's powerful RTX Spark chip

These MacBook Pro rivals pack some seriously impressive tech specs.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: Dell's new laptop trades premium specs for what students might actually care about
item.itunes:title: Dell's new laptop trades premium specs for what students might actually care about
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Dell has begun its IFA announcements with another version of the 14S, just a few months after the DS14260 made its debut earlier this year. Interestingly, rather than trying to one-up its predecessor with more premium specifications, Dell seems to have gone in the opposite direction with the new DS14270.

However, that might not be a bad thing. Dell appears to be trading some of those premium specs for the things students may actually care more about in an everyday laptop.

Dell is focusing on the things students will notice every day

It's built around what students actually need

Credit: Dell

For starters, the new model weighs around 2.5 lbs (equivalent to 1.15kg) and measures just 12.21mm to 13.5mm thick, while still using an aluminum chassis. That’s a pretty noticeable change from the previous 14S, which started at around 1.49kg and measured roughly 15.3mm thick. In other words, Dell has shaved about 300g (or roughly 21%) off the starting weight, while making the laptop slimmer at the same time.

The 14S is available with either a 14-inch 2K 60Hz panel of a sharper 2.8K display with a 120Hz refresh rate. Both use a taller 16:10 aspect ratio, which gives you a bit more vertical space for documents, webpages, and everything else students tend to spend their day staring at. Under the hood, you can choose between Intel’s Core 5 320 and Core 7 350 Series 3 processors.

Dell is also putting a surprising amount of emphasis on the 14s's new battery. The new model uses a higher-density cell that the company says runs cooler under load and retains its capacity over time. Despite the relatively modest 61.2Wh capacity, Dell claims the laptop can manage up to 21 hours of Netflix streaming on a charge.

And for the students who view their technology as a means of expressing themselves (I do too), Dell is leaning much harder into color this time around. The new 14s comes in four finishes: Linen, Dusty Rose, Washed Denim, and Velvet Green. Dell describes this as a deliberate return to more expressive design across its consumer lineup.

  • Credit: Dell
  • Credit: Dell
  • Credit: Dell
  • Credit: Dell
  • Credit: Dell
  • Credit: Dell
  • Credit: Dell
  • Credit: Dell
  • Credit: Dell
  • Credit: Dell

None of those things are going to make the 14S the most powerful laptop in Dell's lineup. But for a student carrying it around campus all day, I'd argue that shaving hundreds of grams off the weight, keeping the battery going for longer, and having a laptop that actually feels a little personal could matter a lot more than having Thunderbolt 4 or a much more capable NPU.

Dell had to make some compromises to get here

Something had to give

Credit: Dell

Of course, making the 14s lighter and potentially more affordable has meant cutting back in a few places. Compared to its predecessor, the differences in the base configuration are hard to miss.

The previous 14S started with a Core Ultra 5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage. This new model instead starts with an Intel Core 5 320 Series 3 processor, 8GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. The NPU takes a particularly noticeable hit too, dropping from 46 TOPS on the Core Ultra 5 322 to just 16 TOPS on the Core 5 320.

Dell has pared back the connectivity as well. Thunderbolt 4 is gone in favor of two 10Gbps USB-C ports, while Wi-Fi 7 has been replaced with Wi-Fi 6 or Wi-Fi 6E depending on the configuration. The battery itself is smaller too, dropping from 70Wh to 61.2Wh, although Dell's claimed battery life suggests that doesn't necessarily translate into worse endurance.

Hands on: The new Dell XPS 13 is a true MacBook Neo killer

It's better everything

2
By  Rich Woods

item.title: Ubisoft bans Linux and Steam Deck users from For Honor because it "cannot meaningfully deploy protection"
item.itunes:title: Ubisoft bans Linux and Steam Deck users from For Honor because it "cannot meaningfully deploy protection"
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Ubisoft blocks Linux and Steam Deck from For Honor on Sept 10, citing anti-cheat limits.
  • This move likely stems from anti-cheat incompatibility, not game performance on Proton.
  • Ubisoft burned goodwill with Linux players, and reopening the platform is uncertain.

Usually, when someone on Linux cannot play an online game, it's down to one of two reasons: either the game doesn't run well despite using Proton, or the game uses an anti-cheat system that's not compatible with Linux. However, this is the first time I've seen a company ban Linux users after years of allowing them to play. Ubisoft has announced that it's going to prevent Linux gamers from playing its title For Honor because it doesn't have the resources to ensure people aren't cheating on it.

Linux and Steam Deck users will be blocked from playing For Honor come September 10th

Sounds like a rough deal for people who enjoyed playing it on the go

As spotted by GamingOnLinux, Ubisoft published a blog post announcing the new Ranked Dominion mode, plus a rework of Ranked Duel, for its 2017 title For Honor. However, the celebrations are cut pretty short when the company follows it up by saying that anyone playing on Linux (and that includes the Steam Deck, which uses the Tux-powered SteamOS) won't be able to play:

"To reinforce a fair competitive environment, the team is introducing additional player safety measures. We are removing For Honor from the Linux platform to ensure a safer environment for our players as we cannot meaningfully deploy protection on this platform. This means that For Honor will no longer be playable on Steam Deck starting September 10th. We will continue to investigate different ways to improve our anti-cheat with the possibility of reopening the platform in the future."

It's likely that Ubisoft couldn't figure out how to make anti-cheat software that would work properly on Linux, so instead of working stuff out, it banned the OS from playing the game online. Here's hoping that Ubisoft does find a way to "reopen the platform" in the future, but honestly, I feel that it has already burned its goodwill with the Linux community with this move.

Linux is still the best option for gamers looking to get away from Microsofts grasp

6
By  Elliot Alexander

item.title: Windows 11 is cluttered by design, so I changed these 4 settings to take back control
item.itunes:title: Windows 11 is cluttered by design, so I changed these 4 settings to take back control
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I first switched over to Windows 11, I realized how cluttered Microsoft's newest OS had become. Between pre-installed AI that I didn't want to use, widgets that promoted clickbait, and prompts to try Microsoft services, I felt inundated with unnecessary content that pulled my focus away from being productive.

That's why I spent some time researching and changing settings so that I could wrestle back a cleaner experience. And while it's not as lean as I would like it to be, changing these defaults made my setup much more manageable.

5 apps that give you the desktop widgets Microsoft won’t

Ditch Windows’ boring widgets! Get real customization with these tools and make your desktop truly yours

2
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

Widgets on the lock screen and taskbar

The biggest source of visual bloat

There are two main places that widgets can appear on Windows 11 — on your lock screen and your taskbar. However, I make sure to disable both so that I don't receive information I'm not interested in.

While widgets can undoubtedly be helpful, Windows 11's customization options leave a lot to be desired. For example, you can't enable the weather widget on your lock screen in isolation. It comes with other widgets like news and financial markets. Meanwhile, the widgets board that appears when you click on your taskbar widget is also filled with irrelevant content.

Rather than deal with the clutter, I disable widgets completely on both my lock screen and taskbar. To disable taskbar widgets, you can head to Settings > Personalization > Taskbar and disable the Widgets toggle.

To disable lock screen widgets, go to Settings > Personalization > Lock screen and make sure that the option under Lock screen status is set to None.

I use these 4 apps to completely customize my Windows 11 PC

Customize Windows 11 the way you want

By  Anurag Singh

Start menu content recommendations

Nothing but a distraction for me

The Start menu is another place that can easily become chaotic with Microsoft recommendations. To avoid this, I make sure to only show my most used apps, and then the rest of my apps in alphabetical order. If you don't turn off recommendations, Windows may recommend apps based on usage, or show you tips about your device. I've never found these recommendations helpful — only distracting.

To disable recommendations, go to Settings > Personalization > Start and turn off the toggle for Show recommendations for tips, shortcuts, new apps, and more. To keep my Start menu clutter-free, I also disable Show recently added apps and Show recommended files in Start, recent files in File Explorer, and items in Jump Lists.

If you don't like the default way the Start menu displays your apps, you can also select a different View. The default is set to Category, which groups your apps together in blocks. I prefer to use List or Grid as I find this makes my Start menu much more manageable.

5 Start menu alternatives and Windows tweaks that will speed up your workflow

Revamp your Windows experience with smarter Start menu alternatives and tweaks—boost efficiency, streamline navigation, and work faster

2
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

Removing pinned apps

No more shortcuts to apps I never use

While this isn't an individual setting, it does involve undoing something Windows 11 does by default for certain apps. I found that my Start menu was cluttered with pinned items I hadn't added, including shortcuts for apps that I had never used.

To get rid of these apps, I was able to right-click on the app and select Remove from Start. For folders, I needed to first click on the folder, drag the apps out of the folder into the pinned section, and then right-click on them to remove them. Eventually, I was able to get rid of the pinned section entirely.

I may pin an app again in future, but right now the way I access my most-used apps is with taskbar shortcuts. Despite me using my PC daily, there aren't all that many apps I need shortcuts to. In fact, it's probably time I cleaned up my taskbar and desktop to eliminate additional clutter.

7 apps that could be slowing your Windows performance

Is your Windows laptop feeling sluggish? These seven apps could be affecting performance.

6
By  Saeed Wazir

Search highlights

Disabling this made my search bar more useful

Search highlights have always felt like a way for Microsoft to push its own content and services to users on Windows 11. These highlights include trending searches, suggested games, and trivia. I don't use Bing as a search engine and I don't really use Microsoft's AI features either. So this entire section is just another bit of clutter on Windows 11.

Rather than being a personalization setting, this option is buried in a different menu. To disable search highlights, I went to Settings > Privacy & security > Search and turned off the toggle for Show search highlights.

This immediately made the search menu interface cleaner and much more useful. Instead of irrelevant content, the menu now includes my top apps and search shortcuts for common queries like display settings.

This reminds me that there are sometimes genuinely useful settings lying beneath the visual bloat, but unfortunately Windows 11 can make it difficult for users to find. In my opinion, this should be the default search menu interface, not the bloated sidebar used to promote Microsoft platforms.

I finally set up ExplorerPatcher on Windows, and I should have sooner

Windows 11 is much better this way

5
By  João Carrasqueira

Changing these settings makes Windows 11 less chaotic

We live in a time when many of us feel constantly advertised to or pushed to use certain services. AI sneaks into your apps and browsers, your PC and smartphone OS are filled with bloatware, and every major tech company wants you to use their preferred services and content providers.

In an effort to end this constant push for my for attention, I've been working to de-bloat my devices and make software experiences less chaotic and cluttered. If you also feel overwhelmed, it might be time to try a change of settings on your WIndows device too.

item.title: I fed my entire Obsidian vault into a local LLM, and now it actually understands my research
item.itunes:title: I fed my entire Obsidian vault into a local LLM, and now it actually understands my research
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Half the time you use any AI for something research-heavy, the opening exchange isn't the question you actually want to ask. Instead, it becomes a whole setup you have to curate first, usually into a folder or project with a system prompt and knowledge base, depending on the AI's workspace features.

This is why Obsidian is one of my favorite note-taking apps, not because it's a phenomenal app, but because the vault already has all the content and background information this type of setup could need, and it's so easy to integrate with just about any tool because of the plain folder structure. All it takes is giving an AI tool filesystem access and pointing it at the vault. And when you use a local LLM instead of cloud AI, the entire pipeline stays private to boot.

Want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI? The XDA AI Insider newsletter drops weekly with deep dives, tool recommendations, and hands-on coverage you won't find anywhere else on the site. Subscribe by modifying your newsletter preferences!

How I hook up my Obsidian to my local LLM

It's a quick MCP server setup

Before I get into how I make this setup work for me, here's what I'm actually working with. I use various LLM runners, but my primary pick is still LM Studio because of how quick and easy it is to spin up, and it also has an easy integration for plugins and MCPs. I use Anthropic's official filesystem server @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem, and my model of choice here is Qwen 3.5 9B because it's what my 8GB VRAM can handle and it's strong at tool calling.

The setup is a single JSON block in mcp.json. You add the filesystem server, point the args at your vault path (double backslashes on Windows), and LM Studio spawns the server on save. One catch is that the server won't start without at least one allowed-directory argument, so if it fails the first time, that's usually why.

What the model actually gets is a small set of file-reading tools. It can list a directory or search filenames, and it can read individual files as full markdown. It's not doing embedding search or RAG. There's no vector database sitting between the model and my notes. It just reads the file when the question needs it, the same way I would. Writes stay on manual approval on my side, since I'm using the vault as read-only memory here rather than letting the model edit anything.

I turned Obsidian into a personal command center, and now I barely open separate apps

My notes, tasks, calendar, research, and writing finally live under one roof.

5
By  Patrick Hearn

My local model has read months of my own research

And it answers like it

I set this up trying to think of it more like a search feature than a document setup, like the model would fetch a note when I asked something specific. And the more you use it, it can also start to feel like long-term memory… that just happens to live on your own PC. I don't keep every single aspect of my life in the vault, at least not in all of them (I have three), but this one has notes, research, pitches, and some random ideas. So now my model basically knows what I know.

The important distinction is that this isn't RAG. Tools like AnythingLLM, Notion AI, and the Smart Connections Obsidian plugin all chunk your notes and embed them into vectors, then retrieve fragments at query time based on semantic similarity. The filesystem MCP hands the model whole files. RAG does scale better for large research stacks, but for the notes I have, the model reading a full note is a way better experience than getting a semantic-match slice of it, because it reads the note the way I wrote it rather than as decontextualized chunks.

That unlocks a class of questions a fresh cloud chat can't really handle. For example, asking whether a tool I tested last month held up when I revisited it: the model pulls the original test note and any daily notes referencing it since, and gives me an actual answer. Or asking whether I've written anything that contradicts what I'm about to write, which catches things I'd otherwise miss. Also useful is asking whether I've touched a tool before when it comes up in the news cycle, and finding out I'd already tested it six months ago in a pitch that never went anywhere. These aren't really fancy capabilities, but definitely practical.

I could just use Claude, but again, local is better for anything you'd rather keep off the cloud. For me that's stuff like finances or embargoed news and so on. It removes any concern you might have about your data ever becoming public.

6 ways anyone can use LM Studio and a local LLM on their PC

Most people can find a use for a local LLM on their PC, and here's how I use mine.

By  Adam Conway

The inverse is also beneficial

The vault got better because I'm pointing a model at it

You'd think that having the vault in your LLM runner is the only benefit here, but I actually found the inverse true as well. If you've read any of my Obsidian-related articles you'll know how I naturally gravitate toward a super messy vault, I'm just that person that stashes stuff and forgets about it. Now having a local LLM inside my vault ended up making it more useful.

Adding content that I knew a model would eventually read forced me to write it more clearly, or at least sort out the frontmatter and wikilinks and such, which a local model also handles easily with write access. So there's a bit of a back-and-forth loop here. For example, if a model keeps retrieving a note about a specific topic but misses the follow-up daily note about my takeaways, I start linking them.

It's almost like the model's retrieval acts like a live audit of my note quality, and if it can't make sense of something I wrote, I probably wouldn't have been able to either in a few months.

I stopped uploading my notes to ChatGPT and NotebookLM after setting up my local LLMs

I ditched cloud platforms for a self-hosted LLM, and my notes have never been more useful

1
By  Ayush Pande

A feedback loop I wasn't expecting

This is such a simple setup but with a huge payoff. Any local LLM session can be turned into a research session so long as the content is already in my vault. Furthermore, you can keep a document in the vault with rules for your local LLM on how to behave, you'll just have to remember to tell it to read that file first because it's not automatic like the mechanics of a claude.md file.

item.title: I stopped buying $70 games after discovering Steam's indie goldmine
item.itunes:title: I stopped buying $70 games after discovering Steam's indie goldmine
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's not a great time to be a gamer of any capacity. PC hardware prices are on the rise, console prices are slowly increasing, and GTA 6 has proven that people are willing to shell out $100 for a game.

Fortunately, despite everything going up in price, I'm still happily gaming. Not only that, but I've also been purchasing brand-new games on release day without breaking my bank account, and the games run perfectly fine on GPUs that aren't RTX 5000 series. If you haven't guessed it yet, I'm talking about the rich, exciting world of weird indie games that live on Steam, which have ensured I never have to pay triple-A prices ever again.

New, cheap, and excellent indie games are releasing every month

Keeping on top of them all is a lot of fun

Valve has introduced two excellent tools to Steam: the Next Fest and the release calendar. The former serves up a smorgasbord of free demos to try, while the latter keeps you up to date on what's on the horizon. The calendar is fantastic for seeing when your wishlisted games are releasing, but it'll also sneak in a few titles it thinks you'd enjoy.

These two tools have made it easier than ever to find the cool new titles that indie devs are working on. I recently picked up IRON NEST: Heavy Turret Simulator, The Message from Deep Space, and Cat Mail Co., entirely because I enjoyed their Next Fest demos, wishlisted them, and then spotted them approaching on my release calendar. And because they're indie titles, they come at a fraction of the price you'd pay for a triple-A game.

I ditched my gaming PC for cloud gaming when hardware prices spiraled out of control

It's not perfect, but it's a solution.

2
By  Simon Batt

Some indie games are a regularly maintained labor of love

Their update schedule beats that of triple-A titles

Another cool element of Steam is that it lets you peek at a game's update history before you purchase it. This is especially useful for Early Access titles, so you can gauge whether a game is still in active development. In fact, Valve added a warning to Early Access titles that hadn't received a substantial update in a few months to address this problem.

If you look deep enough, you'll find some games that will give you a huge amount of progressive entertainment for your money's worth. Personally, I think Devil Spire Falls is at the top of the list of indie games that just grow and grow over time. Every week, the developer adds a new patch to the game. The patch is usually more than just bug fixes; it'll often add new in-world elements, spells, or races for you to play. It's not unusual to leave the game alone for a month, then come back and see that the developer has added a ton more content for you to explore.

"Friendslop" games have given my social group hours of fun

I honestly use that term lovingly

In case you haven't heard, there's a new genre of game that's been making the rounds lately. It's called "friendslop," and it's a weird case where you can use it either as a slur or as praise. The genre essentially boils down to a cheap online multiplayer game that uses simple graphics and mechanics to produce something quickly, and whether you find that delightful will likely define how you view the term "friendslop."

Personally, I love these kinds of games, and my friends do, too. That's why we hoard games that cost around $5-10 (but we can go as high as $20 if we really like a game) and then play them on a rota. We beat one, put it aside, and then find something else to do. When the game receives an update, or there's a cool mod we want to try, or we just miss the game itself, we'll dig it back up and play it again.

This means my friend group has a very deep pool of titles we can draw on at any time. A game we haven't played in a year got a huge content update? Time to fire it up. A friend expressed interest in playing it for the first time? Make a new save file. Do you just find the game a blast to play and your 'replay cooldown' has expired? Now you have your weekend plans sorted.

My group has replayed Escape the Backrooms so many times because it has matched all three of those conditions at different times, meaning we got a ton of playtime for a very good price point. It's not something I can say for triple-A games, which are usually a 'one-and-done' affair.

item.title: This open-source tool was built for academics, and it's the best productivity tool I own
item.itunes:title: This open-source tool was built for academics, and it's the best productivity tool I own
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Some of the best productivity tools aren't the ones designed for the job I'm using them for. I have often picked up an app because it solves one specific problem, only to slowly adjust it around my own workflow. Open-source software makes this even more common because I can use a tool in ways its creators may never have expected.

That's exactly what happened with Zotero. It was built with academics in mind, but I found myself using it for much more than citations or academic work. The more I used it, the more naturally it fit into my everyday workflow. What started as a niche tool ended up becoming one of my favorite ways to stay organized.

Zotero is much more than a citation manager

It became more than I expected

I originally installed Zotero because I kept seeing it recommended as a citation manager. I assumed that was its entire purpose. After spending some time with it, I realized the citation side is only one part of what makes it useful.

What surprised me was how well Zotero handles information. It gives me a structured place to bring things together without forcing me to build a complicated system around them. I can keep related information connected, add context when I need it, and move between different pieces of information without losing the thread.

I use Zotero to keep track of articles I want to revisit

I stopped losing useful articles

One of the simplest ways I use Zotero is to save articles that I know I will want to read again. I come across plenty of useful articles while researching a topic, but I don't always have time to read them properly. Instead of leaving them open in a browser tab, I save them to Zotero and move on.

This has become useful when I find something that isn't immediately relevant to the article I'm writing. It might explain a technology well, cover an interesting development, or simply give me an idea I want to explore later. I can save it without having to decide what I will do with it right away.

I also like that saving an article doesn't interrupt my workflow. The browser connector lets me add it to Zotero in a couple of clicks, so I don't have to copy the title, URL, or other details manually. Over time, this has given me a much better place for articles I want to revisit than my browser's bookmark folder ever did.

Zotero and Obsidian just became the most powerful research duo, thanks to this plugin

Zotero-Library-in-Obsidian brings all of your research into your vault.

1
By  Patrick Hearn

Zotero has become my research library

I built my own research library

The more I used Zotero, the more I started treating it like my own research library. Instead of thinking about individual sources, I began organizing information around the subjects I regularly write about. This made it easier to build a useful collection of material over time.

For example, when I'm working on a topic like self-hosting, AI, or productivity software, I can keep everything related to that subject together. I don't have to create a new system every time I start researching something. I simply add useful material to the relevant collection and continue working.

I also like that my research stays separate from the actual writing process. Zotero is where I gather and organize the material, while my writing tools are where I turn that material into an article. Keeping those two things separate makes my workflow feel much less cluttered.

The biggest change is that I no longer think of research as something that ends when an article is published. The material I collect can remain useful for future projects, giving me a growing library that I can return to whenever I need it.

The PDF and annotation features

I get more from every PDF

The PDF support is another reason Zotero has stayed in my workflow. I often download manuals, reports, research papers, and other documents while working, and Zotero gives me a convenient way to work with them without opening another app.

What I find most useful is being able to highlight parts of a document and add notes directly to it. I also use annotations when I'm reading longer documents. Rather than trying to remember where I saw something useful, I can leave a short note beside it. Later, I can return to the document and quickly understand why I marked that particular section. For me, this makes Zotero useful during the actual reading process, not just as a place to store documents.

4 Zotero plugins that are my productivity secret weapon

Zotero, but better

I stopped thinking of Zotero as an academic tool

Zotero wasn't designed for the way I use it today, but that is exactly what makes it interesting. I don't need to be a student or researcher to get value from a tool built around managing information properly. It has quietly become one of those apps I rely on whenever I don't want useful information to disappear into the mess of everyday work. I simply wanted a better way to keep track of things, and Zotero turned out to be surprisingly good at it.
